chunks: Muhammad ibn Ya'qub from Ali ibn Muhammad from Ibrahim ibn Ishaq from Muhammad ibn Sulayman from Abdullah ibn Sinan who said:

Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) said: "Indeed, the charity of the leather shoe and the hoof is given to those Muslims who adorn themselves; as for the charity of gold and silver, and that which is measured by the qafiz, and that which the earth produces, it is for the needy who are poor."

Ibn Sinan said: I said, "And how did this become so?" He said, "Because these [those with shoes/hooves] adorn themselves and are modest before people, so the more beautiful of the two matters is given to them in the eyes of people, and both are charity."

key_terms.أَجْمَلُ الْأَمْرَيْنِ: The more beautiful of the two matters
key_terms.الْفُقَرَاءِ الْمُدْقَعِينَ: The needy who are poor/in dire need
key_terms.الْقَفِيزُ: A traditional unit of volume measurement for grain

ai.seo_question: What is the difference in zakat distribution between gold/silver and agricultural produce or livestock in Shia jurisprudence?
ai.summary: In this narration from *Tahdhib al-Ahkam*, Imam al-Sadiq (AS) elucidates the wisdom behind categorizing zakat recipients by distinguishing between 'al-mutajammilin' (those who adorn themselves, often interpreted as the broader community or those with moderate means who value dignity) and 'al-mudqi'in' (the destitute). The Imam explains that giving adornments to the former preserves their social modesty and honor, as they are less likely to be stigmatized for receiving luxury items, whereas essential goods are reserved for the truly needy. This highlights the Shia scholarly emphasis on *hikmah* (wisdom) and social psychology in zakat distribution, ensuring that charity uplifts rather than diminishes the recipient's status.
